statement: 3 lemons cost 12 cents altogether. Every lemon costs the same. How much do 5 lemons cost?

choices.misconception: I found the price of one lemon and stopped there.
I added the price of just one more lemon, which gives the cost of 4 lemons.
I added 5 cents to 12 cents because there are 5 lemons.
I treated 12 cents as the price of one lemon and multiplied it by 5.

hints: When every item costs the same, find the price of one item first by sharing the total. Then build up the price of as many items as you need.
12 cents shared between 3 lemons is 4 cents each. Now count up 5 lemons at 4 cents each.

solutions.reliable: 3 lemons cost 12 cents, so one lemon costs 4 cents, because 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Then 5 lemons cost 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20 cents. The idea to keep: go through the price of one item, then count up.
solutions.elegant: 5 lemons are 3 lemons plus 2 more. The 3 cost 12 cents and 2 more cost 8 cents, so 12 + 8 = 20 cents. The idea to keep: split the new amount into a part you already know and a small extra part.

whyOnTest: Going through the price of one is the first step to all rate problems, and each wrong choice skips or reuses a number.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
